author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 against the v2 quality gate
basis: Full rewrite. The earlier overlay still failed eight of twelve slides and soft-missed three quarters of them, mostly by running under the 20-second fill floor and below the A2 Flesch-Kincaid band, and several slides repeated the B1 wording almost word for word. This text is written from the source meaning in present-simple spoken English, one idea per sentence, with a because-clause on slide 5 and a before-clause on slide 9 so the A2 grammar is visible, and no participle clauses, clefts or fronting. Meaning, slide order and every named fact are unchanged: SDG 9, the United Nations, ChatGPT, Gemini, AI slop, the four parts of a prompt (role, background, goal, limit). Facts corrected: the workbook says the model 'only guesses the next word' and 'does not understand your ideas'. A language model predicts the next word, and it works only from the words in the prompt plus the patterns in its training text, so slide 5 says it never reads your mind and only sees the words you type. Slide 12 ends on the claim: the workbook's 'Thank you' was cut, because it kills the applause line.

slides.1: Good morning. Today we look at SDG 9, a world plan from the United Nations. It helps every country build better factories and support modern science.
slides.2: AI is changing science very quickly. It also changes the way we share our ideas. But the answer always depends on one thing: exactly how we ask.
slides.3: Many science students use ChatGPT or Gemini. We fix our lab reports, we read short summaries, and we ask about hard homework. It is very quick and easy.
slides.4: This tool is really handy. But some students only type a few lazy words, and the reply is boring and empty. People call this AI slop.
slides.5: Why does this happen? The computer never reads your mind, because it only sees the words in your prompt. Few details always bring a weak answer.
slides.6: A useful prompt has four parts. Give the model a role, and give it the background facts. Then add your goal and a simple limit.
slides.7: Clear writing really matters in science. A careful prompt improves the lab reports and the talks that we hand in. Our study also gets quicker and more correct.
slides.8: But never copy an answer without thinking. If you do, you will simply stop learning. Real science starts with human wonder, and never with a fast reply.
slides.9: So think before you type. Ask yourself exactly what you really need, and decide who will finally read your report. Then pick the format that fits.
slides.10: Then give the machine clear orders. Add your student background, and add the exact format you want. Writing a prompt is science communication too.
slides.11: Computers can sort a lot of data very well. But they have no wonder, no instinct and no honest heart. Only people really turn numbers into new discoveries.
slides.12: Good ideas always start with good talking. Better prompts bring better answers. But a careful scientist still has to think about every single word.
